shows.title: Les mains
shows.description:
Constantin Nitsche's second show with Xavier Hufkens takes its title from a line in one of Kafka's letters to Milena Jesenská — "I can't hold enough of you in my hands" — and that sense of grasping at something that keeps slipping away runs through every canvas. Painted in his Marseille studio through a process of layering, revision and partial erasure, the works let earlier compositional decisions survive as ghostly traces beneath the final image, so a painting like Nature morte au melon reads as several attempts collapsed into one.

The exhibition moves between self-portraiture, still life and domestic fragments — a Ficus plant, a yellow floral screen, pink flowers recurring across canvases, and Nitsche's wife appearing throughout as a constant presence. Two paired works, Les mains and La main, mirror each other around an exchanged flower, and a self-portrait of the artist as Pinocchio, painted before one of his favourite works by Whistler, plays with the idea of self-portraiture as construction rather than simple likeness. Nitsche's long-standing interest in Kafka and in the darker undertow of German fairy tales gives even his quietest still lifes a faint charge of unease.

The paintings favour restraint over resolution — Nitsche talks about stopping at the point where one more gesture would diminish rather than deepen the image — and the results feel suspended rather than finished, closer to a mood caught mid-sentence than a settled statement.

shows.title: Summer Group Show
shows.description:
Galerie La Forest Divonne's Brussels space closes out the summer with its annual mixed hang, pulling together painting, sculpture, and works on paper by the roster of French and Belgian artists the gallery represents across its Paris and Brussels programs. Expect the gallery's signature tone: figuration and landscape painting handled with a painterly, tactile touch, alongside sculptural and ceramic work that plays off texture and material.

Summer group shows like this one function as a survey of the gallery's current thinking — a chance to see how painters such as Vincent Bioulès sit next to sculptors and object-makers in the program, without the pressure of a single curatorial thesis. It's a low-key, browsable exhibition, well suited to a slow August visit to the gallery's Avenue Louise space before the more thematic autumn programming begins.

shows.title: Pigments et Présence
shows.description:
Lita Albuquerque has spent five decades pressing raw pigment directly into landscapes — deserts in California and Egypt, ice in Antarctica — so it's a change of register to see her work indoors, at intimate scale, in this selection of drawings, prints and paintings spanning the 1980s to today. As a founding figure of the Land Art and Light and Space movements, Albuquerque helped bring saturated, often mineral color into a genre that had mostly worked in earth tones and shadow; this show distills that project down to works on paper and panel that can fit inside a gallery nave rather than a stretch of desert.

The drawings, all untitled and made by pressing loose pigment straight onto paper with her hands, carry the same gesture she has used outdoors for years — the artist's touch left visible in the material itself, rather than mediated through a brush. The large paintings, worked in gold resin, extend her signature ultramarine blue (first used to color a line cut into the Malibu hillside in 1978) into a luminous, almost devotional surface that shifts with the light in the room.

Seen together, the works make the case that Albuquerque's outdoor interventions and her studio practice have always been two expressions of one interest: the physical, alchemical charge of pure pigment, and its capacity to connect body, landscape and cosmos. It's a rare chance to see the raw material of her large-scale earthworks handled at human scale.

venue.name: La Patinoire Royale \u2013 Galerie Val\u00e9rie Bach

shows.title: Lost and Found. Japanese Photography at the A Foundation
shows.description:
This group exhibition draws entirely on Fondation A's own photography holdings, supplemented by a deliberate effort to bring forward women photographers who have historically been left out of the canon of Japanese photography. The show opens with an installation by Takahashi Munemasa built from family snapshots recovered from the wreckage of Yamamoto, a town devastated by the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami — water-damaged, mud-stained pictures of ordinary domestic life that give the whole exhibition its title and its emotional register of things half-lost, half-recovered.

From there the exhibition moves between two poles of catastrophe and vitality that have shaped Japanese photography since the postwar period. On one side are photographers who have returned again and again to the afterimage of the atomic bombings and subsequent disasters — Ishiguro Kenji, Miyako Ishiuchi and Tsuchida Hiromi on Hiroshima, Miyamoto Ryūji and Shiga Lieko on the Kobe earthquake and the 2011 tsunami. On the other are bursts of unruly color and spectacle from the 1970s and 80s: Shibuya Noriko's images of the flamboyant Takenoko-zoku street dancers, Sugimoto Tatsuki's crowds at Aomori's Nebuta festival, and the formal experiments of Araki Nobuyoshi, Takanashi Yutaka and Yamazawa Eiko.

Curated by Julien Frydman, the exhibition is less a survey than an argument: that Japanese photography's fascination with rupture and its appetite for exuberant renewal are two expressions of the same restless relationship to a world that keeps threatening to disappear. Narahashi Asako's half-submerged self-portraits, floating between sea and sky, offer a fitting emblem for a show that keeps its subjects — and its viewers — permanently off balance.

shows.title: A Gift of Tears
shows.description:
Robert Martin's first European solo show brings together paintings, watercolors and a wood-and-steel installation built around a single emotional premise: that grief, tenderness and wonder sharpen rather than dull our sense of connection to the world. The title nods to the old Christian idea of the "gift of tears," but Martin treats it as a description of feeling itself rather than a religious claim.

Nature does a lot of the work here — trees, birds, water and shifting skies recur across the paintings, often tied to specific memories (a divided tree trunk, a returned fawn, migrating birds) that Martin uses as stand-ins for loss, resilience and the instability of "home." A suite of eight watercolors borrows the geometric structure of stained glass, a visual language Martin absorbed from churches he visited in Ghent while working on this body of work, though the sacred imagery here is repurposed to elevate the natural world rather than any doctrine.

The show's centerpiece, a mural of painted and sculpted geese that spreads off the wall and into the gallery, is the most literal expression of Martin's idea that home is found through movement rather than fixed geography. It's an ambitious, personal debut, heavy with autobiography but resistant to easy sentimentality.
shows.reception: Wednesday, September 2, 6-9pm (preview); RendezVous Brussels Art Week opening Thursday, September 10, 6-9pm

shows.title: Summer Escape
shows.artist: Sabine Nielsen, Sander Reijgers, Jef Aerosol, Zenoy, JC Thorez, Mireille Liénard, Thierry Malty
shows.description:
Summer Escape gathers seven artists from Galerie Martine Ehmer's roster for a loose, warm-weather group hang that spans the gallery's split identity between urban art and contemporary painting. Street-art veterans Jef Aerosol — known for his stencilled figures and musicians — and the more graphic, pattern-driven Zenoy anchor one wing, their work rooted in the Belgian urban-art scene the gallery has championed for over a decade.

Alongside them, painters Sabine Nielsen, Sander Reijgers and JC Thorez bring differing takes on abstraction and color-field-adjacent composition, while sculptor and mixed-media artist Mireille Liénard and painter Thierry Malty round out the show with more textural, material-driven pieces — Malty's flame-toned canvases in particular read as a counterpoint to the cooler, graphic work elsewhere in the space.

As a summer group show, the exhibition doesn't argue a single thesis so much as offer a survey of the gallery's current stable, useful for anyone wanting a quick read on the range of contemporary and urban art coming out of this Waterloo space since its 2025 move south of Brussels proper.

shows.title: Nathalie Amand: Photo-montages
shows.description:
Nathalie Amand works the way a collector works: combing flea markets and old-paper fairs for discarded documents, magazines and ephemera, then reworking them into new images by layering in her own photographs. The results sit somewhere between collage and palimpsest — surreal, frankly sexual botanical scenes where bodies merge with plants, mannequins sprout flowers, and antique print stock becomes the ground for new, invented anatomies.

This show doubles as the launch of Le Carnet rose, a book pairing texts by the writer Jacques Sojcher with Amand's photo-montages, published in La Pierre d'Alun's La Petite Pierre collection. The pairing makes sense: both artist and writer are working a vein of exuberant, slightly transgressive eroticism dressed up in the vocabulary of gardens and growth — flowers, ferns, butterflies, vines standing in for desire that's never subtle about what it's after.

It's a small, idiosyncratic show suited to Le Salon d'Art's own hybrid identity as a hairdressing salon that has run a serious exhibition and small-press publishing program on the side for fifty years. Amand's work — playful, explicit, visually dense — fits comfortably into that tradition of treating a commercial storefront as a real exhibition space rather than a backdrop.

shows.title: Vanishing Point
shows.description:
Hans Op de Beeck's first solo show with Almine Rech turns the gallery into one of the artist's signature grey-scale mental landscapes. Expect the furniture, tableaux and figures he is known for — a life-sized sculptural figure titled Cécile paired with an earlier polyester seascape — all rendered in the chalky, ash-toned palette that strips objects of period and place. The show also folds in an animated film of the same title, in which interiors and figures dissolve and reassemble in slow, hypnotic sequence.

Op de Beeck has spent two decades building quiet, theatrical scenes — hotel lobbies, dinner tables, carousels — that look almost real until a small distortion gives away their constructed nature. "Vanishing Point" leans into the idea of classical perspective as a metaphor: a horizon that organizes the eye even as it recedes from grasp. It's a fitting frame for an artist whose work is fundamentally about suspended time and unresolved narrative.

For anyone who knows Op de Beeck from museum-scale installations, this is a chance to see the more intimate, sculptural side of his practice in a commercial gallery setting — dense with atmosphere but built at human scale.

shows.title: Diary of Happiness
shows.description:
Jean-Michel Othoniel's first major Brussels exhibition spreads more than a hundred works — glass sculptures, garden installations and rarely-shown watercolors — through the salons, bedrooms and gardens of the Villa Empain, turning the Art Deco house into something closer to a travel diary. Each room is keyed to a country that has shaped Othoniel's work over three decades: Armenia, Belgium, Italy, the United States, France, India, Japan, Turkey. The effect is cumulative rather than thematic, more scrapbook than survey.

Othoniel is best known for his blown-glass beads and necklaces, scaled up into public sculpture (his Kiosque des Noctambules for the Paris metro is probably his most famous work), and that vocabulary of luminous, knotted glass forms carries through the monumental pieces installed in the Villa's pool and gardens. What's less expected here is the density of works on paper — roughly a hundred watercolors, many never exhibited before, that read as a private, almost diaristic counterpoint to the glasswork's public spectacle.

Because the show is built around the specific architecture of the Villa Empain — an Art Deco landmark in its own right — it rewards slow movement through the house as much as attention to any single object. It's as much about inhabiting a building as it is about viewing sculpture.

shows.title: Shape of Absence
shows.description:
This project-space show, curated by Louma Salamé, takes on the destruction of Syrian cultural heritage since 2011 through a single, quietly devastating installation. Hrair Sarkissian's Stolen Past arranges 48 lithophanes — thin, backlit panels made from a 3D-printed bioplastic — like funerary stelae, each one revealing a faint black-and-white image of an artifact looted or destroyed at the Raqqa museum, which lost all but 880 of its roughly 8,000 objects when ISIS controlled the city between 2013 and 2017.

Sarkissian, who trained in his father's photography studio in Damascus before becoming one of the more prominent conceptual photographers of his generation, uses a mid-19th-century printing technique here rather than straight photography — a way of literally making absence visible, translucent, and slow to read. Paired with the installation are immersive 3D-scanned images from Iconem documenting the ruins of Palmyra, offering a second register of loss: not looted objects but an entire archaeological site eroded by conflict and time.

It's a small, somber show, more about memory and documentation than spectacle, and it sits at the more political end of what the Villa Empain usually presents.

shows.title: Veils of Light
shows.description:
Jonathan Adolphe (1952–2022) built paintings out of urethane, fiberglass, smoke and powdered pigment rather than paint proper, casting translucent skins over images that stay half-hidden beneath the surface. "Veils of Light" gathers a group of these luminous, scarred panels, in which light and obscured imagery do most of the emotional work rather than any figurative subject.

Adolphe described his own method as drawing with smoke and poured urethane — an "abstract writing" aimed at things like fog, ice, steam and sweat, materials chosen specifically because they resist being pinned down. Early in his career he had already been mixing painting with sculpture, working wax, sand and chalkboards into hybrid objects; the mature works here push that same impulse toward something closer to devotional objects, pale and glowing rather than declarative.

It's a quiet, materially strange body of work, and a good match for a gallery that has spent recent seasons alternating between decorative art fair fare and more considered solo shows like this one.

shows.title: Sophie Kuijken
shows.description:
Sophie Kuijken's Brussels solo show gathers recent paintings, several of which appeared in her recent retrospective at the Centre d'art contemporain Matmut - Daniel Havis in France, and introduces a new circular format — the tondo — into her practice for the first time in about twenty years. It's a small formal pivot for an artist whose whole career has been built on a single, narrow obsession: the portrait.

Kuijken doesn't paint from life. She builds her figures from a decades-deep personal archive of images scraped from the internet, cutting and reassembling legs, eyes, hands and props until a face emerges that belongs to no one in particular. The results are faces that feel plausible and slightly wrong at the same time — a hand bent at an odd angle, an outfit that doesn't quite match an era — which is precisely the uncanny territory she's after. She trained at KASK in Ghent, then spent over twenty years working in near-total withdrawal from the art world before her first museum show in 2011 at the Dhondt-Dhaenens brought her out of it.

The tondo format adds an extra layer worth noticing: an ancient, Renaissance-associated shape that also happens to mirror the circular crop of a social media profile picture, which suits an artist whose entire method is already about the internet-age remixing of found faces into invented ones.

shows.title: Takayuki Sakiyama
shows.description:
Takayuki Sakiyama has spent nearly four decades coaxing clay into shapes that behave less like pottery than like frozen weather. Working from a studio overlooking the Izu Peninsula, he throws vessels and then tears, folds, and pleats their walls while the clay is still soft, so that a finished piece reads as a wave caught mid-break or a dune ridge sculpted by wind. His signature sand glaze, fired to a matte, granular finish in warm beige and sun-bleached tones, reinforces the illusion that these are geological fragments rather than thrown forms.

This is Sakiyama's third exhibition with the gallery since 2015, and it gathers a new group of his sand-glazed sculptural vessels. The interiors and exteriors of these pieces blur into one continuous surface, a effect that has become the throughline of his mature work: there is no clear boundary between inside and outside, only a single undulating skin. Seen together, the group reads like a small tidal landscape, each piece a distinct gesture within one long study of erosion and motion.

For anyone interested in contemporary ceramics that lean toward sculpture rather than the decorative arts, this is a rare chance to see a significant body of Sakiyama's work in Brussels, in a gallery that has represented his practice for over a decade.

shows.title: Casual/Tease
shows.artist: Reza Aramesh, Julieta Aranda, Kader Attia, Nina Berman, Julian Charrière, Baptist Coelho, Detex, Kendell Geers, Shilpa Gupta, Dan Halter, Majd Abdel Hamid, Mona Hatoum, Hideyuki Ishibashi, Benoît Jacquemin, Will Kerr, Lesia Khomenko, Kapwani Kiwanga, Daria Koltsova, Vera Kox, Anton Kusters, Rachel Labastie, Emilio López-Menchero, Edgar Martins, Ismail Matar, Aimé Mpane & Jean Pierre Müller, Pratchaya Phinthong, Walid Raad, Shareef Sarhan, Omid Shirazi, Laure Tixier, Danh Vō, Meltem Yildiz, Mohammad Zaza, Zgjim Zyba
shows.description:
Casual/Tease arrives at Cloud Seven as part of The Memorial for Those Who Did Not Fall in War, a traveling curatorial project developed by Columbia University's Global Center for Peace Innovation. Curator Hadas Zahavi has assembled a large international roster of artists around a single, quietly unsettling idea: that the imagery of war trains us to look for casualty in rubble and dust, while missing the violence embedded in ordinary, undisturbed scenes.

The works on view stay close to the surface of everyday life — a window view, a household ladder, a handmade ceramic vessel — and let each object slowly reveal a second, darker reading, whether that's a drone's-eye view disguised as a garden outlook or a grenade shape hidden in domestic ceramics. The through-line connects distant, sanitized sites of military decision-making (laboratories, boardrooms, trade routes) to the people who go on living, working and breathing amid the long aftermath of conflict.

With more than thirty participating artists spanning photography, sculpture, video and installation, this is a dense, research-driven group show rather than a quick visual hit — worth the time it asks for, given how deliberately it works against the numbing effect of war imagery we're used to scrolling past.

shows.title: Old DNA
shows.description:
Old DNA is the Dutch sculptor Folkert de Jong's first solo exhibition with Galerie Christophe Gaillard, opening the gallery's Brussels space for Rendez-Vous Brussels Art Week. De Jong has spent two decades building a body of sculpture out of foam, pigment and resin, using unstable, almost toxic-looking synthetic materials to make figures that feel both historical and radioactive — soldiers, dandies and allegorical bodies rendered in queasy candy colors.

The title points to his long-running preoccupation with how power, violence and spectacle get encoded and re-encoded across generations, as if certain postures and hierarchies were passed down like genetic material. Expect large-scale figurative sculpture that continues his signature vocabulary of camouflage-bright surfaces and theatrical, slightly grotesque staging, alongside newer works that push the material and palette further.

De Jong has shown at major institutions across Europe and the US, and this exhibition marks a first chance to see a substantial, focused presentation of his work in a commercial Brussels gallery. The artist gives a guided tour in English on the opening Saturday of the fair weekend.

shows.title: On a Shelf
shows.description:
Nathalie Du Pasquier made her name in the 1980s as a founding member of the Memphis Group, and she has spent the decades since translating that design sensibility into painting — flattened still lifes of invented objects, stacked forms and geometric fragments that read like blueprints for furniture that was never built. On a Shelf gathers new paintings that continue this vocabulary: compositions built from simple volumes, bold flat color and a faint sense of domestic order, as if each canvas were a shelf holding a small, private collection of shapes.

Du Pasquier's work sits at the border between abstraction and object-painting; her forms suggest vessels, tools and architectural fragments without ever settling into recognizable things. The paintings on view continue this play with scale and arrangement, using a restrained palette and careful, almost obsessive composition to turn ordinary pictorial furniture into something quietly strange.

Presented alongside Marina Pinsky's concurrent show at the gallery, this is a chance to see one of design and painting's more distinctive crossover figures still working at full strength, more than four decades into her career.

shows.title: The Wave(s) or Newton's Rings
shows.description:
Marina Pinsky works across sculpture and photography, often using the language of scientific and architectural documentation — measured grids, cross-sections, riverbeds, calculators — to make objects that sit somewhere between diagram and artifact. The Wave(s) or Newton's Rings takes its title from the optical interference pattern that appears when light bounces between two curved surfaces, a nod to Pinsky's ongoing interest in how vision, measurement and material intersect.

Her recent work has drawn on found urban and geological material — riverbeds, pebbles, sections of buildings — translating them into cast and constructed pieces that keep one foot in document and one in sculpture. Expect a similarly hybrid approach here: works that look like they could be scientific specimens or architectural fragments, presented with the cool, precise staging that has become her signature.

Pinsky, who trained in Brussels and has shown internationally, treats the gallery as a kind of laboratory for testing how images and objects translate into and out of each other. This show runs alongside Nathalie Du Pasquier's concurrent exhibition at the gallery.

shows.title: The Atavists
shows.description:
Tinus Vermeersch paints a world that feels excavated rather than invented, populated by hybrid creatures, bird-men, and figures caught mid-ritual in landscapes that seem to belong to no specific era. His technique matches the content: he works in oil on panel using deliberately old-fashioned, time-consuming methods, drawing on a deep knowledge of historical craft and folkloric imagery from indigenous and animist traditions.

This new body of work continues the surreal mythology Vermeersch has been building across drawing, tempera, sculpture and installation for years. Familiar figures from his private cosmology, like the enclosed, shell-like "Tegumen" form and the recurring bird-man archetype, appear again here, but transformed: the Tegumen is broken open, and floral and plant motifs move into the foreground, merging and decaying in tangled clusters. Small boats carrying anonymous figures drift through several works, suggesting migration, ritual, or simply passage through an ambiguous world.

The show's title plays on "atavism," the reappearance of ancestral traits skipped over by intervening generations, and it applies equally to Vermeersch's subjects and his method: a deliberate reactivation of older techniques and older stories rather than a straightforward look backward. The paintings are dense, quiet, and unsettling in equal measure, rewarding the kind of close looking that reveals new detail with every pass. Vermeersch's work is held in institutional collections including the Museum of Ixelles and the Belfius Collection, and this is his latest solo presentation with Hopstreet.

shows.title: Le Choc de la couleur
shows.description:
Vincent Bioulès has spent decades painting the landscape and light of the south of France, and this show — its title translates as "the shock of color" — gathers recent canvases built from saturated, unmixed color: acid greens, hot pinks, and deep blues laid down in confident, economical strokes. Mimosa branches, mountain views, and garden scenes recur, treated less as observed motifs than as excuses for color to do the work.

Bioulès came up through the Supports/Surfaces circle in the 1970s, and even in these late, warmly representational landscapes you can feel that formalist training in how flatly and directly the paint sits on the canvas — color as structure, not just description. The exhibition brings together large-format views alongside smaller, more intimate still lifes, giving a good sense of the range within what is otherwise a tightly focused body of work.

shows.title: Un flic sous l'Occupation
shows.description:
Galerie Champaka's autumn show is built around original pages from Jean-Michel Beuriot's new series with longtime writing partner Philippe Richelle, a police procedural set in occupied Paris during the Second World War. Beuriot, a Belgian draughtsman best known for the acclaimed "Amours fragiles" cycle, works in a restrained, classical clear-line style — carefully staged interiors, controlled lighting, and faces drawn with a novelist's attention to small gesture.

The exhibited plates follow three police inspectors investigating a brutal double murder that leads them into the murky economy of collaboration, black-market fixers, and criminals working for the German occupier. It's genre comics with real historical weight: Beuriot and Richelle have built a substantial body of work together mining France's wartime compromises, and seeing the original boards up close reveals just how much storytelling is carried by his framing and use of shadow rather than dialogue.

For a gallery devoted to comic art in the heart of the Sablon, this is a fairly typical program: a serious, mid-career bande dessinée artist given a proper spotlight on the work behind the printed album.

shows.title: Caminhos
shows.description:
Marcos Siqueira paints from close, sustained looking: the geometry of branches and leaves, the shifting angle of light through the day, the shadows one hill casts on another around the Serra do Cipó in Brazil, where he lives and works. This new body of paintings, grounded in that landscape, keeps circling back to a central question about the difference between observing the world and imagining it — and whether imagination might simply be what observation becomes once it has had time to settle into memory.

The paintings themselves resist easy description. Figures balance impossibly on wires strung to fallen poles; ghostly, shadow-bodies sit at either end of small boats on rivers that seem to run straight into the night sky; beams of light move through bare branches like independent, animate things. Siqueira mixes his own pigments from earth gathered on the paths he walks daily, so the material of the paint is literally of the place it depicts, even as the images drift toward the uncanny and the spectral.

This is Siqueira's first exhibition at Mendes Wood DM's Brussels space, and it arrives as a suite of nocturnal, dreamlike scenes that reward the same patient attention the artist brings to his subjects — paintings built less to be glanced at than to be stood in front of for a while.

shows.title: Shed: Works on Paper
shows.description:
Nat Meade's first solo show with Nosbaum Reding in Brussels is built entirely around works on paper, a shift from the artist's usual painting practice that gives the exhibition its loose, exploratory feel. Working in casein tempera, Meade renders modest, semi-abstracted scenes — a shed, a porch, a stack of forms — that hover between domestic interior and psychological space.

The title plays a double game: a shed is the improvised, unglamorous structure where families accumulate tools and memories, but "shedding" is also the act of letting go, of shrugging off inherited forms to make room for something new. That tension runs through the whole body of work, where sparse, blocky figures and structures seem to be caught mid-transformation, neither fully built nor fully dissolved.

Meade's palette is muted and chalky, in keeping with casein tempera's flat, matte finish, and the works on paper have an unfinished, provisional quality that suits their subject matter. It's an intimate introduction to an artist known for pushing figuration toward something stranger and more schematic, shown here at a smaller, more vulnerable scale than his paintings usually allow.

shows.title: BOLERO
shows.description:
Kristof Santy's second solo show at Sorry We're Closed takes over all three floors of the gallery with a body of new paintings, drawings and, for the first time in his practice, three-dimensional works on copper plate. The title nods to Ravel's famous score: a piece built entirely on repetition and gradual intensification rather than narrative, which is exactly how Santy wants his pictures to be read. Flowers, dishware, kitchen taps, interiors and other unremarkable domestic objects recur across the works, flattened and rebuilt through pattern, saturated color and insistent repetition until they tip from the mundane into something stranger and more monumental.

Santy, a self-taught Belgian painter who worked in a factory before turning fully to art, has built a reputation over the past several years for this kind of deadpan, folk-inflected realism, with echoes of Ensor, Magritte and Belgian modernist painting filtered through a flea-market sensibility for overlooked objects. His work has been shown recently alongside major names at institutions including S.M.A.K. in Ghent and the Heidi Horten Collection in Vienna, and this exhibition arrives on the back of that momentum with what the gallery describes as a major new body of work accompanied by a dedicated publication.

Given the scale of the show — spread across three floors with new mediums entering the mix — it's a useful checkpoint for anyone following how far Santy can stretch a deliberately narrow vocabulary of everyday things before it becomes purely a matter of rhythm and form.

shows.title: I Wish I'd Taken More Photographs
shows.description:
This is Isaac Andrews's first solo exhibition, and it arrives as a fairly confident debut: nine oil paintings built around flattened, wallpapered interiors that read less like rooms than like stage sets for feeling. There's no single light source in any of these pictures, and that's the point — Andrews isn't trying to convince you a scene is real, he's using pattern, saturated color and cropped, cinematic framing to put a mood on the canvas directly.

The largest and title work, along with paintings like What Was Left and You Are Love, cycle through desire, loneliness and togetherness using the same vocabulary of decorative surfaces and fractured domestic space. A recurring motif of flowers — sometimes barely legible as such against fields of oxblood and burgundy — threads through several canvases as a shorthand for growth, decay and the general unpredictability of being alive, with Dear April standing out as the most explicitly floral and tender of the group.

It's a small show in terms of object count but a coherent one, more interested in accumulated atmosphere than any single showstopper painting, and worth seeing as an early data point on an artist whose palette and interiors already feel distinct.

shows.title: People Are Strange
shows.description:
Kasper Sonne's second solo show with Maruani Mercier gathers new paintings of solitary, elegantly dressed figures set against oceans and skies rendered in thinned, luminous layers of pigment on unprimed linen. The clothes are quotations lifted from fashion imagery and social media, and Sonne uses them as a kind of camouflage: his subjects read less as individuals than as constructed images of contemporary identity, caught between belonging and estrangement.

Water is the recurring ground note of the series — a horizon line, a threshold, occasionally a direct nod to art history, as in a reworking of Manet's balcony paintings. Sonne has spoken about the sea as both beauty and menace, and that ambivalence carries into the pictures, which pair reclining nudes and upright, watchful figures with skies that feel more psychological than meteorological.

Formally, the appeal is in the buildup: numerous thin washes on raw linen create a shimmering, stained-glass surface that Sonne then interrupts with passages of thick, worked impasto around the figures' clothing and features. The result sits somewhere between figurative painting and abstraction, and rewards close looking as much as it does a first glance across the gallery.
shows.reception: Thursday, September 10, 2026, 4-9pm, in the presence of the artist

shows.title: The Failure of Order
shows.description:
Nicolás Lamas builds his exhibitions out of collisions — found objects, photographic fragments, and constructed sculptures pushed together until their original functions and meanings start to short-circuit. The Failure of Order brings together sculpture, photography, assemblage and installation around the idea that disorder and uncertainty aren't failures of a system but built into it: every attempt to classify or measure the world quietly generates the very complexity it was meant to contain.

Lamas has long worked as a kind of amateur archaeologist of the present, pairing industrial materials, geological specimens and obsolete technology in arrangements that look provisional and precise at once. Here that method is turned toward questions of cognition and representation directly — what happens in the gap between a model of reality and reality itself, and what escapes every system built to capture it.

It's a cerebral premise, but the work tends to land through simple, often witty material juxtapositions rather than didactic explanation. Expect an exhibition that asks to be walked through slowly, where objects that look at first like studio debris reveal themselves as carefully calibrated arguments about knowledge and its limits.

shows.title: El Pulso del Agua — Part II
shows.description:
Nils Verkaeren doesn't paint landscapes so much as wrestle with them. Over eight years he carried canvases into the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, the Amazon, Los Llanos, and along the Río Magdalena, Río La Miel and Río Cauca, letting rain, humidity, river sediment, and heat work directly on the paint surface. The resulting works are less pictures of a place than physical residues of time spent in it, records of a body and a canvas moving through terrain most painters would never bring materials into.

This Brussels presentation, staged as part of Rendez-Vous Brussels Art Week and running as the second half of a two-city diptych with a concurrent painting-focused show in the gallery's new Antwerp space, turns away from the finished canvases to show the expedition itself: field recordings, sketches, notebooks, photographs and archival material documenting the logistics and physical toll of working in remote, difficult conditions. It's a rare chance to see the research infrastructure behind a body of work, alongside a selection of the paintings themselves.

Verkaeren's practice sits somewhere between plein-air painting and endurance art — his surfaces are shaped as much by weather and river water as by his own hand. Shown together with the accompanying monograph published by Hopper & Fuchs, this is a meditative, unusually process-driven look at what it means to paint a landscape by actually living inside it.

shows.title: Couleur – Matière – Énergie
shows.description:
Robert Brandy has been painting independently since 1972, a fifty-year career built almost entirely outside institutional categories. Trained partly under Vincent Bioulès, whose Supports/Surfaces circle taught him to stretch his own canvases and grind his own pigments, Brandy took that hands-on relationship to materials and turned it into a lifelong method rather than a period style. This show, titled for the three things that have driven his work throughout — color, matter, energy — brings recent paintings to Galerie Faider alongside the launch of a new artist's book, Tiercé Gagnant: Couleur – Matière – Énergie, with text by the critic Roger-Pierre Turine.

Brandy's practice has moved through recognizable phases, from spare, almost ascetic canvases early in his career to freer, more gestural work built around washes of ink and saturated color. What holds constant is an insistence on the physical fact of paint — its texture, its resistance, the visible trace of the artist's hand — over any fixed pictorial program. At an age when many painters settle into a signature look, Brandy's recent output reads as restless and additive, closer to an ongoing experiment than a closing statement.

The book launch, with a print run of numbered and signed copies accompanied by an artist's proof, underscores how much Brandy has treated publishing and painting as parallel tracks over the decades; this exhibition is as much a chance to see the work gathered in print as it is to see it on the wall.

shows.title: Liturgie des jours
shows.description:
Two Ukrainian artists share the gallery's central nave for a show built out of daily ritual under sustained war. Sasha Kurmaz's contribution is Red Horse, a piece he has been making every single day since Russia's full-scale invasion began in 2022: a collage of found photographs, scraps of cardboard, handwritten notes and his own pictures, hundreds of individual sheets that together form one long, unfinished diary. He calls it a diary of life rather than a diary of war — the point being that the mundane and the catastrophic have become impossible to separate. The first 462 collages, laid out in a single continuous line, are shown here; the project itself won the Grand Prix Images Vevey and the Kraszna-Krausz Photography Book Award after being published as an 800-page book.

Danylo Halkin works with a different kind of material memory. His Optical Prostheses series is built from stained glass salvaged from his home region of Dnipropetrovsk — windows that once hung in hospitals, fire stations and recruitment offices, now sold as architectural salvage after missile strikes destroyed the buildings that held them. Halkin also paints monochrome versions of windows that no longer exist at all, stripping out the color but keeping every compositional detail, so that a lost object survives as a ghost image rather than a photograph.

Put together, the two practices approach the same problem — how ordinary things carry the trace of a war that refuses to end — from opposite directions: Kurmaz through accumulation and repetition, Halkin through salvage and translation. It's a demanding, meditative show, closer to bearing witness in real time than to looking back at history.

shows.title: Another Life
shows.description:
Alvin Ong's new paintings emerge directly from a personal low point — a burnout the Singaporean artist has spoken about openly — and it shows in the way bodies in this work keep dissolving and doubling. Faces blur into translucency, figures blend into each other, and heads split into fractured, multiple versions of themselves, as if recovery meant living several lives at once rather than returning cleanly to one.

Ong's palette and motifs draw on the religious imagery he grew up around: rhinestones embedded in the paint surface and passages of text recall devotional objects, while recurring screens implicate the viewer as someone watching, rather than simply looking. The strongest new thread is Residues, a series painted onto found antique shop signs and blinds sourced in Singapore, where fragments of old lettering and imagery are worked back into the composition alongside the artist's own invented scenes — painting as a layering of found history and private narrative.

Eyes are conspicuously blanked out or omitted throughout the show, a small but insistent refusal that runs through even the most tender images here. Taken together, the paintings read less as illustrations of a breakdown than as a way of imagining alternate selves — the "other lives" of the title — that might have been lived instead.

shows.title: Dressage Ruined by Puffers
shows.description:
Lisa Vlaemminck's paintings start from an unusual decision: instead of putting an image on a rectangular canvas, she cuts the support itself into a shape — a tooth, a hairstyle, a slice of cheese, a chicken leg — and then paints something onto it that may have nothing to do with that silhouette. The tension between a recognizable outline and an unrelated image is the whole engine of the work; a contour that reads instantly as "cheese" might carry a painted scene that undercuts or ignores that reading entirely.

The results sit in the gap between object and picture. Vlaemminck draws her source material from still-life painting, advertising and the general visual clutter of consumer life, where objects are already selected, staged and charged with meaning beyond their function. Food and body parts recur as subjects precisely because they carry that same charge of attraction and repulsion — things we want to consume, touch or otherwise possess, pushed slightly past comfort through repetition and odd juxtaposition.

There's a structural, almost game-like logic to how the show is built, one the artist has compared to cellular automata — simple local rules generating unexpectedly complex patterns as shape, image and material bump against each other across the room. A newly written text by Febe Lamiroy, composed alongside the paintings in the studio, accompanies the exhibition as a kind of verbal counterpart to Vlaemminck's visual displacements.

shows.title: Le temps suspendu
shows.description:
Jacques de Loustal has spent decades building one of the most recognizable visual worlds in French-language illustration: hushed hotel rooms, tropical ports, solitary drinkers, and long nocturnal journeys rendered in warm, saturated color. This exhibition draws together several strands of his practice at once — paintings, charcoal drawings, glass-backed fixés, nude studies, and a major suite of illustrations made for the "Le Monde" newspaper's collected editions of Georges Simenon's novels.

The Simenon connection is the show's spine. Loustal has long been drawn to the novelist's fascination with atmosphere over incident, and his black-and-white cover illustrations for the Simenon series translate that same attention to mood, discretion, and melancholy into image form; several are shown here alongside color reworkings that open the compositions up in new ways. A parallel body of charcoal drawings, tied to a new monograph on that side of his practice, shows a quieter, more tonal register: deep blacks, velvety grays, and a use of untouched paper as light, drawing on a tradition of observational landscape drawing.

Taken together, the exhibition argues for the coherence of Loustal's work across media — whether in ink, charcoal, oil, or glass, the same eye for framing, silence, and the poetry of in-between moments (a bar before closing, a hallway before someone enters) runs through everything. It's a rich survey for anyone who knows Loustal from his comics work and wants to see how that sensibility extends into drawing and painting.

shows.title: C'est vous que ce village là-bas attend pour s'éveiller à l'existence
shows.description:
Adrian Geller paints flowers, empty houses and quiet still lifes as a way of asking what's left to look at once the belief systems that used to give objects meaning have fallen away. In his own extended statement for the show, he describes painting as an act without doctrine — a way of attending closely to the world's beauty without needing to anchor it in symbolism, faith or explanation.

The paintings draw on a scattered set of references: Gustave Roud's writing on lost, half-mythical villages, T.S. Eliot's Hollow Men, and the artist's own preoccupation with objects that persist after the systems that once gave them significance have collapsed — empty houses, unoccupied shells, bouquets that are no longer vanitas but simply themselves. It's a quietly philosophical body of work, more interested in the space between belief and reason than in resolving it.

Formally the work stays close to traditional still life and landscape painting, but the ideas behind it push toward something more open-ended: paintings as places "awaiting a presence" rather than fixed images with settled meaning.
